title: Supervision-Adaptive Curriculum and Guarded Anti-Curriculum Learning for Dense Prediction

paper.title: Supervision-Adaptive Curriculum and Guarded Anti-Curriculum Learning for Dense Prediction
paper.abstract: Abstract Curriculum learning orders samples by difficulty, but difficulty alone does not establish supervision reliability for dense prediction. Easy samples can expose shortcuts, hard samples can be informative, and noisy or ambiguous samples can mislead training. Building on our conference method CurriSeg, we present PaceShift, a stabilize-then-challenge paradigm combining supervision-adaptive curriculum selection with guarded spectral post-training. A learning-dynamics view motivates separating supervision reliability from temporal update value and applying spectral challenges after stabilization. The first phase estimates reliability from available supervision, augmentation consistency, model disagreement, and prediction certainty. Temporal statistics guide sample weighting, while pixel-uncertainty weights reduce the early influence of uncertain regions. The second phase ranks predictions from multiple spectral views using supervision agreement, robustness, reference consistency, and penalties. A pairwise preference objective measured against the frozen Phase-I reference, together with an anchor, refines the prediction. The framework supports full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision. Experiments across context-entangled content segmentation (CECS), broader dense-prediction tasks, and foundation-model and cross-modal adaptations show accuracy gains. Targeted diagnostics indicate improved pooled calibration and corruption robustness in the evaluated settings. PaceShift preserves the deployed architecture and adds no inference computation. Code will be publicly released.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Dense prediction assigns a structured label to every pixel and underpins perception across medical, autonomous, and industrial applications [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Most progress has been architectural: stronger backbones [ 6 ] , dedicated detectors with multi-scale aggregation [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , attention [ 10 ] , and frequency-aware modules [ 11 ] . We instead argue that dense prediction is limited not only by network capacity but also by training-signal reliability and the order in which it is consumed (Fig. ). Fig. 2: Curriculum paradigms for dense prediction. A naive curriculum orders samples easy-to-hard by a static ground-truth difficulty and can strengthen reliance on fragile texture cues. CurriSeg adds temporal statistics and a stabilize-then-challenge schedule, but its score is defined by dense-mask error and its single-radius challenge is unguarded. PaceShift keeps the same overall two-phase training skeleton and changes two core components: a four-cue supervision-adaptive score ρ i \rho_{i} and a guarded multi-radius spectral challenge during post-training, without changing the deployed model architecture. The reliability problem is sharpest in context-entangled content segmentation (CECS), where objects share intrinsic visual patterns with their background, as in camouflaged object detection [ 7 ] , transparent object detection [ 12 ] , and concealed defect detection [ 4 , 13 ] . We also include polyp segmentation as a CECS-related task with low boundary contrast, local ambiguity, and annotation uncertainty. Existing methods address the resulting feature ambiguity mainly by enhancing representations [ 11 , 14 ] . Yet a more basic bottleneck is the learning dynamics that arise when the data distribution is entangled. We make this concrete with three observations that, while most visible in CECS, recur across dense prediction. Difficulty and learning value are not the same quantity. Curriculum learning [ 15 ] typically orders samples from easy to hard, but in CECS, apparent easiness can arise from residual texture contrast that reveals the object. Prioritizing samples with low loss or error may therefore encourage reliance on fragile high-frequency cues instead of shape and context. This concern is supported by our experiments: under a matched budget, naive easy-to-hard ordering performs no better than random ordering, while conventional schedules can reduce accuracy. Frequency-intervention results further show greater sensitivity to high-frequency perturbations after naive easy-first training. Hard samples pose a complementary challenge: high prediction error can reflect either informative visual difficulty or unreliable supervision. A well-concealed object may be difficult yet informative, whereas weak annotations, imperfect ground-truth quality [ 16 ] , label drift, or intrinsically ambiguous regions can produce high errors without equally useful training signals. Since a static difficulty score cannot reliably distinguish these cases, difficulty-based selection may discard informative samples while retaining unreliable ones, increasing the risk of overfitting. Confidence, finally, is not reliability. Uncertain boundary and low-contrast regions can dominate early gradients, while high confidence need not imply correctness. Directly rewarding confidence can therefore reinforce errors and degrade calibration. Together, these three observations suggest that reliable training must distinguish supervision quality from temporal learning value, regulate uncertain pixels, and challenge shortcut reliance only after initial stabilization is reached. From CurriSeg to PaceShift. Our conference work CurriSeg [ 17 ] , published at ICML 2026, introduced a two-phase stabilize-then-challenge framework for CECS. It combined dense-mask difficulty trajectories, temporal sample weighting, pixel uncertainty weighting, and single-radius spectral-blindness fine-tuning (SBFT). However, its difficulty score required dense ground-truth masks and could not be applied uniformly across weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision. Moreover, its single-radius spectral stage lacked a mechanism for assessing the reliability of alternative predictions. To address these limitations, we develop PaceShift (Fig. 2 ), which retains the two-phase design while introducing supervision-adaptive curriculum selection and guarded multi-radius post-training with reference-relative preference learning. These changes extend the training framework without modifying the deployed architecture or increasing inference cost. Scope. CECS serves as our primary setting for studying supervision reliability and texture shortcuts together. Experiments on broader dense-prediction tasks evaluate the transfer of the full training framework, while mechanism-specific evidence is established primarily in CECS and unreliable-supervision settings. This paper makes four contributions: (1) A learning-dynamics view of dense prediction (Sec. III-B ). We explain why naive easy-first curricula can amplify fragile shortcuts and why the stabilize-then-challenge framework succeeds, separating supervision reliability from temporal update value and treating SBFT as a post-stabilization frequency bottleneck whose order matters. (2) Supervision-adaptive curriculum selection (Sec. III-C ). We replace ground-truth difficulty with a reliability score combining available supervision, augmentation consistency, model disagreement, and prediction uncertainty, yielding one curriculum under full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision while reducing confirmation bias. (3) Guarded anti-curriculum post-training (Sec. III-D ). SBFT-P (SBFT with preference-guarded post-training) combines multi-radius spectral challenges with a supervision-adaptive preference guard based on correctness, robustness, and consistency, with uncertainty as a weak penalty and not as the sole selection rule, improving robustness while reducing overconfidence in the evaluated settings and recovering the original SBFT as a special case under full supervision. (4) Systematic validation and diagnostics (Sec. IV ). We evaluate PaceShift across multiple dense-prediction families, supervision regimes, architectures, data-centric baselines, and foundation-model and cross-modal settings. Targeted experiments examine training dynamics, supervision reliability, candidate selection, corruption robustness, and calibration without additional inference computation. Beyond the methodological changes, this journal extension substantially expands the evaluation of CurriSeg [ 17 ] . We extend the broader dense-prediction evaluation to clinical, dichotomous, and salient segmentation; add vision-language and reference-guided evaluations; expand data-centric comparisons; and report paired-run statistical tests. Targeted analyses of supervision reliability, temporal update value, guard selection, phase ordering, frequency sensitivity, corruption robustness, and calibration further examine the underlying mechanisms.

sections.heading: II Related Work
sections.text: Context-entangled and dense prediction segmentation. CECS spans camouflaged object detection [ 3 , 18 ] , transparent object detection [ 19 ] , and concealed defect detection [ 13 ] , with polyp segmentation [ 20 ] as a closely related low-contrast task. Progress has been mostly architectural: encoder-decoder backbones with multi-scale aggregation [ 7 ] , attention-based refinement [ 9 ] , edge- or uncertainty-aware branches [ 10 , 21 ] , transformer context modeling [ 22 ] , and frequency-aware modules [ 11 ] . These works strengthen representation but keep a standard supervised routine with shuffled mini-batches, so the roles of sample difficulty, label ambiguity, and texture shortcuts in the learning dynamics remain underexplored. Reversible unfolding [ 12 ] and nested unfolding [ 14 ] designs have begun to inject inductive structure into the decoder, yet the optimization schedule itself is rarely treated as an explicit design variable. Curriculum learning and self-paced learning. Curriculum learning orders training from easy to hard to improve generalization [ 15 , 23 ] , with variants in self-paced learning [ 24 ] , teacher-student curricula [ 25 , 26 ] , and loss- or hardness-based ranking [ 27 , 28 ] . These methods assume that easy samples give reliable supervision and that difficulty tracks learning utility. Both break in CECS: easy samples may carry spurious texture that promotes shortcuts, and hard samples can be at once informative and ambiguous, consistent with analyses showing that the benefit of ordering depends sharply on data structure [ 26 ] . Most curricula also ignore the pixel-level uncertainty of dense prediction, and almost none deliberately increase difficulty after a stable solution is reached. PaceShift instead separates reliability from temporal update value, extends the curriculum to pixels, and introduces a post-stabilization anti-curriculum. Data-centric learning: training dynamics and data efficiency. Training-dynamics methods characterize examples through evolving predictions, losses, margins, or gradients, including forgetting events [ 29 , 30 ] , EL2N and GraNd [ 31 ] , dataset cartography [ 32 ] , and AUM [ 33 ] . Dyn-Unc [ 34 ] and TDDS [ 35 ] further exploit temporal variability, while InfoBatch [ 36 ] and SeTa [ 37 ] dynamically remove low-value samples for efficiency. ADELE [ 38 ] instead uses early-learning dynamics to correct noisy labels. Most of these formulations assume sample-level labels and do not directly address sparse, pixel-level, or model-derived supervision. PaceShift builds on this line of work but derives the trajectory from supervision-adaptive dense reliability, couples it with pixel-level uncertainty, and follows stabilization with guarded post-training. Its aim is accuracy, robustness, and calibration under spatially and supervision-dependent unreliability, not pruning or label correction. Learning under incomplete supervision. Weakly and semi-supervised segmentation learn from sparse annotations or unlabeled data through consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling [ 39 , 40 ] . A recurring failure is confirmation bias: training on the model’s own confident predictions reinforces existing errors [ 41 ] . In CECS this is acute, since confidence and correctness diverge in concealed regions, so a confidence threshold both keeps wrong pseudo-labels and discards hard but correct ones. PaceShift instead combines confidence, disagreement, consistency, and an external foundation-model cue for reliability estimation, whereas SEE [ 42 ] generates changing pseudo-labels from a frozen SAM and SCALER [ 43 ] jointly adapts SAM and the segmenter. Shortcut bias, texture bias, and frequency-domain learning. Networks trained by SGD favor the simplest features that separate the data even when more robust ones exist, studied as simplicity bias [ 44 , 45 ] and, for vision, texture bias [ 46 ] . This differs from the spectral bias of network functions, which learn the low-frequency components of the input-output map first [ 47 ] . The two concern different frequencies, image versus function, and conflating them yields contradictory predictions about a low-pass operation. We therefore frame SBFT as suppressing a high-frequency image shortcut to counteract texture bias without invoking function-space spectral bias. Foundation-model adaptation and post-training. Segment-Anything-style models [ 48 ] are adapted to specialized domains through adapters, prompt modules, or low-rank updates [ 49 , 50 ] . Related segmentation systems condition on text or image prompts [ 51 , 52 ] , open-vocabulary alignment [ 53 ] , or reference images [ 54 ] . Such conditioning introduces another source of unreliability, namely the alignment between the conditioning signal and the predicted mask, which PaceShift treats as an additional reliability cue without adding a new mechanism. Separately, DPO [ 55 ] learns from preferred and dispreferred outputs without fitting a separate explicit reward model. We adopt a related pairwise objective for dense predictions and define preferences through correctness, robustness, and consistency on dense masks. Fig. 3: Framework of PaceShift. Top (schematic): performance rises in Phase I, is perturbed by the spectral challenge at T c T_{c} , and settles higher in Phase II. Phase I (SA-RCS) : four reliability cues form a supervision-adaptive difficulty d i = 1 − ρ i d_{i}=1-\rho_{i} . After a warm-up on all samples, a percentile curriculum selects 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} , and TSSW and PUE reweight the loss at sample and pixel level. Phase II (SBFT-P) : a multi-radius challenge yields candidates that a guard scores into a preferred and dispreferred mask, refined against the reference θ 0 \theta_{0} . No inference parameters are added.

sections.heading: III-B A Learning-Dynamics View
sections.text: We first lay out the learning dynamics motivating the design.

sections.heading: III-B 1 Easy samples amplify a high-frequency shortcut
sections.text: In a context-entangled scene, an object is concealed when its appearance matches the background. In CECS, one recurring source of apparent easiness is residual local high-frequency texture contrast that separates the object from its background. A model trained on these first can minimize the loss by keying on that texture difference, a feature that is cheap to fit and locally discriminative but does not transfer to well-concealed cases. This is an instance of simplicity and texture bias [ 44 ] : gradient descent prefers the simplest separating feature even when a more robust shape or context feature exists. This is not the classical spectral bias of network functions [ 47 , 56 ] , which concerns the order in which frequencies of the input-output map are learned. Here the relevant frequency is in image space, and the pathology is that early easy-first training increases reliance on a high-frequency image cue. This motivates the two phases: keep shortcut-prone easy samples from dominating early training, then suppress the high-frequency channel once a sufficiently stable representation exists.

sections.heading: III-B 2 Temporal dynamics reveal update value
sections.text: A single difficulty value cannot tell an informative hard sample from a noisy one, while the training trajectory can. For sample i i let d i ( k ) d_{i}^{(k)} denote its difficulty at checkpoint k k . Two patterns are used as heuristics. A high variance of { d i ( k ) } k \{d_{i}^{(k)}\}_{k} reflects strong temporal variation, which is common near decision boundaries or under intrinsic ambiguity. A high mean with low variance reflects persistent failure, which can arise from outliers or label errors that the model cannot resolve, and the empirical rule down-weights it. This reading aligns with example-difficulty and forgetting analyses [ 29 , 31 ] and with Dyn-Unc and TDDS [ 34 , 35 ] , which likewise exploit training dynamics instead of a single value. We import neither score directly: we model the mean, the variance, and the persistent-failure pattern of high mean and low variance as separate, individually ablatable terms on the supervision-adaptive difficulty of Sec. III-C , because the noise-ambiguity dilemma of CECS requires distinguishing all three under any supervision regime. This is what motivates the parameter-free mid-variance preference and the outlier penalty ω out \omega^{\mathrm{out}} in Sec. III-C : intermediate temporal variation serves as a heuristic for potentially informative hardness, whereas persistent stability and persistent failure are down-weighted.

sections.heading: III-B 3 SBFT is a post-stabilization frequency bottleneck
sections.text: Split the input into a low-frequency component x lo x^{\mathrm{lo}} and a high-frequency component x hi x^{\mathrm{hi}} . A representation useful for dense prediction should retain the information needed for the target without relying on the nuisance channel x hi x^{\mathrm{hi}} . SBFT attenuates x hi x^{\mathrm{hi}} while requiring consistent prediction through the supervised or guarded objective, a frequency-level bottleneck inspired by, but not formally an instance of, the information bottleneck [ 57 ] . The phase order is not interchangeable: if the bottleneck is imposed before a stable representation exists, the model is deprived of the cues it needs to bootstrap structure, and applying the challenge directly after warm-up falls below standard training on every reported metric (Table XXII ).

sections.heading: III-C Supervision-Adaptive Robust Curriculum Selection
sections.text: SA-RCS targets the noise-ambiguity dilemma by monitoring the temporal behavior of samples and the spatial uncertainty of pixels, and it does so without assuming a complete mask. It has four parts: a warm-up curriculum, a supervision-adaptive difficulty, a temporal sample weighting, and a pixel uncertainty weighting, combined in a single loss.

sections.text: For a sample i ∈ 𝒮 t i\in\mathcal{S}_{t} the loss combines the two granularities, ℒ curr = ω i ​ ℒ seg w ​ ( y ^ i , t i , W i ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{curr}}=\omega_{i}\,\mathcal{L}^{w}_{\mathrm{seg}}(\hat{y}_{i},t_{i},W_{i}), (9) where ℒ seg w \mathcal{L}^{w}_{\mathrm{seg}} is the regime-appropriate weighted segmentation loss, a weighted BCE plus IoU under full supervision, the corresponding scribble, point, or box loss under weak supervision, and an entropy-gated pseudo-label loss for unlabeled samples, applied to the matching supervision-adaptive target t i t_{i} . Trust follows the primary supervision source, with the supervision-specific definitions given in the Supp.

sections.heading: III-C 6 Beyond binary masks
sections.text: Multi-class and instance segmentation need no new component: the binary entropy becomes a normalized multi-class entropy, agreement is measured by class-averaged IoU or by Hungarian-matched mask IoU with an object-count term, and the degeneration penalty penalizes collapse to background, onto a single class, or in object count. The trust and loss coefficients τ trust \tau_{\mathrm{trust}} , ε \varepsilon , and λ anc \lambda_{\mathrm{anc}} are shared, with fixed output-specific collapse checks detailed in the Supp., and Eqs. 4 , 6 and 3 transfer unchanged: they operate on the scalar d i = 1 − ρ i d_{i}=1-\rho_{i} and never see the output format.

sections.heading: III-C 7 Cross-modal conditioning
sections.text: Conditioning on a language prompt or a reference image adds one axis of unreliability: the mask may disagree with the conditioning even when the model is internally confident. We instantiate the existing cues rather than introducing new ones, leaving ρ i \rho_{i} and Q ⁡ ( m ) Q(m) unchanged and s i sup s_{i}^{\mathrm{sup}} mask-level. Language conditioning uses prompt-paraphrase consistency, the agreement across semantically equivalent rephrasings, and vision-text disagreement, the gap to a vision-only prediction. Reference conditioning analogously uses reference-swap consistency and vision-reference disagreement. Conditioned predictions provide reliability evidence, not fixed training labels, while the trust level continues to follow the primary supervision source (Table I ).

sections.heading: III-E Overall Training Pipeline
sections.text: PaceShift leaves the architecture unchanged and adds no inference cost, with modest overhead incurred only during training and the full procedure listed in the Supp. Overhead. Modest training overhead comes only from the periodic augmented and stochastic forward predictions that refresh the Phase-I reliability cues, and from the spectral-candidate and frozen-reference evaluations of Phase II. The temporal history stores one scalar per refresh checkpoint per sample in memory, and the reduced active subset in Phase I offsets part of the extra computation (Table III ). Hyperparameter footprint. All reliability and guard weights derive from the trust level τ trust \tau_{\mathrm{trust}} of Table I . The mid-variance map is parameter-free, the preference and temperature scales are both fixed to one, β ⁡ ( t ) \beta(t) follows the prescribed schedule, and T c T_{c} admits an adaptive trigger with comparable performance ( Table XXII ). The remaining global constants p min p_{\min} , w min w_{\min} , ε \varepsilon , and λ anc \lambda_{\mathrm{anc}} are fixed once and reused unchanged across all tasks, backbones, and regimes, while H H and the phase boundaries follow the common budget-scaling rule in the Supp. Sensitivity is reported in the Supp., and no per-dataset tuning is used.

sections.heading: IV-A Experimental Setup
sections.text: Tasks, datasets, and metrics. We group three core CECS tasks and the related polyp-segmentation task into the CECS suite: camouflaged object detection (COD) on CAMO [ 64 ] , COD10K [ 1 ] , CHAMELEON [ 65 ] , and NC4K [ 66 ] , polyp image segmentation (PIS) trained on Kvasir [ 67 ] and ClinicDB [ 68 ] and evaluated on CVC-ColonDB [ 69 ] and ETIS [ 70 ] , transparent object detection (TOD) on GDD [ 19 ] and GSD [ 71 ] , and zero-shot concealed defect detection (CDD) on CDS2K [ 13 ] . We further test broader generality across infrared small-target detection ( IRSTD-1k [ 72 ] ), shadow detection ( SBU [ 73 ] ), medical lesion and fluid segmentation ( ISIC 2018 [ 74 ] and RETOUCH [ 75 ] ), dichotomous and salient segmentation ( DIS-VD [ 76 ] and DUTS-TE [ 77 ] ), and semantic ( ADE20K [ 78 ] ) and instance ( COCO [ 79 ] ) segmentation, and supervision generality under point and semi-supervised settings, foundation-model adaptation, and language- and reference-conditioned segmentation. For COD, we report mean absolute error ( M M ), adaptive F-measure ( F β F_{\beta} ) [ 80 ] , mean E-measure ( E ϕ E_{\phi} ) [ 81 ] , and structure measure ( S α S_{\alpha} ) [ 82 ] . PIS uses mean Dice, mIoU, and S α S_{\alpha} , TOD uses mIoU, F β max F_{\beta}^{\max} , and M M , and CDD adds the mean F-measure ( F β m F_{\beta}^{m} ) to the COD metrics. Other tasks use their standard metrics. We assess calibration using pixel-pooled ECE [ 83 ] . We also report a ground-truth-stratified confidence–accuracy gap ( GT ​ - ​ CAG \mathrm{GT\text{-}CAG} , the mean of the gaps computed on ground-truth foreground and background pixels), a boundary-restricted gap ( CAG bnd \mathrm{CAG}_{\mathrm{bnd}} ), and WConf, the mean confidence on incorrectly predicted pixels. These three are complementary diagnostics of where confidence departs from accuracy, not measures of global calibration, since a calibrated predictor can have a nonzero stratified gap. sections.heading: IV-C Generalization across Architectures
sections.text: PaceShift replaces a training schedule, not a module, so it should compose with any segmenter. Table VIII attaches the identical recipe, with identical global constants, to thirteen configurations of twelve detectors spanning encoder-decoder, graph, bio-inspired, frequency, attention, uncertainty, diffusion, unfolding, and foundation-model designs. Each baseline keeps its own backbone, optimizer, and augmentation, and only the training recipe changes. Six rows reuse runs reported elsewhere: FEDER, FSEL, RUN, and the two NUN rows are the COD10K results of the canonical runs in Table II , and the SAM-Adapter row repeats Table XIV . The remaining seven detectors are trained under their native epoch budgets with the phase boundaries scaled as in the Supp. Three observations follow. (1) Every configuration improves, within a band of 3.8 3.8 to 6.5 6.5 percent, and PaceShift exceeds CurriSeg on all thirteen rows. (2) It is complementary to architectural modeling of the very quantities it controls: UGTR already reasons about uncertainty inside the network and is nonetheless among the larger beneficiaries, and FSEL, which models frequency, still gains, because such a module changes how features are computed while the schedule changes what training signal the optimizer receives . (3) The gains persist under the adaptation regime that is replacing task-specific training: DINO V2 and the frozen SAM adapter improve by 4.3 4.3 and 4.7 4.7 percent without any change to their adapters or frozen weights.

sections.heading: IV-D Generalization to Broader Dense Prediction Families
sections.text: To assess PaceShift beyond CECS, we evaluate increasingly diverse dense-prediction tasks exhibiting high-frequency shortcuts, supervision-reliability variation, both, or neither prominently (Sec. III-B ). Tier 1 collects low-contrast detection with ambiguous annotation, Tier 2 low-contrast clinical dense prediction, and Tier 3 salient object detection and dichotomous segmentation with standard semantic and instance segmentation, the last using the multi-class instantiation of Sec. III-C . For each family, Table IX keeps one strong published baseline’s architecture, optimizer, augmentation, and epoch budget, changes only the training strategy with no constant retuned, and reports the family’s primary metric. Tier 1: low-contrast detection with ambiguous annotation. Infrared small-target detection (IRSTD) and shadow detection are low-contrast but not texture-matched, and both carry substantial annotation ambiguity [ 73 ] . Gains persist here although the texture shortcut is weaker, indicating that the full formulation is not limited to shortcut-dominated data. Tier 2: clinical dense prediction. Skin lesion and retinal OCT fluid segmentation combine low boundary contrast with costly, uncertain annotation, making supervision quality and boundary ambiguity particularly relevant to the reliability formulation. On RETOUCH, CurriSeg falls marginally below the baseline, whereas PaceShift recovers this loss and further improves performance under the same clinical setting. Tier 3: standard dense prediction. Dichotomous, salient, semantic, and instance segmentation are not defined by a texture-matched background. PaceShift nevertheless yields consistent gains under the native host budgets, with the same proportional stabilize-then-challenge schedule and without introducing task-specific constants. The multi-class and instance rows use the corresponding output-form instantiations of Sec. III-C . These results support transfer of the full training paradigm beyond context-entangled settings.

sections.heading: IV-H Results on VLM- and Reference-Guided Segmentation
sections.text: A growing family of segmenters uses vision-language or reference information. We apply PaceShift to three such settings for controlled comparison, each with the original baseline and a stronger recent method, preserving the architecture, input protocol, optimizer, training horizon, and trainable parameter count while changing only data scheduling and post-training. Each setting is evaluated on its native benchmark with the corresponding official metrics. The unreliability PaceShift addresses is instantiated per case. The conference recipe is compared in the CECS and incomplete-supervision experiments, and this section reports PaceShift against the host baselines. VLM-based weakly supervised segmentation. CLIP-based segmenters derive supervision from CAM pseudo-masks whose quality varies widely across images and classes. Since no dense GT exists at training time, the difficulty stays d i = − ρ i d_{i}\!=\!1\!-\!\rho_{i} , with class-balanced CAM agreement serving as the supervision signal s i sup s_{i}^{\mathrm{sup}} , vision-language evidence entering through the consistency and disagreement cues of Sec. III-C , and normalized multi-class entropy completing ρ i \rho_{i} , so pseudo-mask reliability is assessed from several decoupled cues instead of CAM confidence alone. Table XV plugs PaceShift into WeCLIP [ 110 ] and ExCEL [ 111 ] on PASCAL VOC [ 116 ] and MS COCO [ 79 ] , with DIAL [ 109 ] for context, improving both models on every evaluated split. VLM-based open-vocabulary camouflaged segmentation. Open-vocabulary segmentation requires both localizing camouflaged objects and recognizing potentially unseen classes. We incorporate vision-language agreement into the existing disagreement and consistency cues, while Q sup Q_{\mathrm{sup}} uses available mask supervision for each candidate. Table XVI shows that PaceShift consistently improves OVCoser [ 113 ] and COCUS [ 114 ] , including class-aware IoU. The generic FC-CLIP [ 112 ] performs worse on OVCamo, highlighting the difficulty of this task for general-purpose segmenters. Reference-guided camouflaged segmentation. Reference-target agreement provides condition-specific reliability evidence during training, computed in an independent feature space so it does not merely echo the segmenter’s own matching branch, and enters through the same cues. Table XVII plugs PaceShift into R2CNet [ 54 ] , which introduced the R2C7K benchmark, and the stronger RefOnce [ 115 ] , which distills references into a prototype memory and needs none at inference. Both improve consistently on every metric.

sections.heading: IV-K Mechanism Analysis
sections.text: We next assess whether ρ i \rho_{i} tracks supervision quality, ω i \omega_{i} reflects update value, Q ⁡ ( m ) Q(m) ranks better candidates, and spectral post-training reduces high-frequency reliance.

sections.heading: IV-K 1 Does reliability track supervision quality
sections.text: In the triage of Table XIII , the full ρ i \rho_{i} gives the best corruption detection and retained quality. Removing the external proposal lowers AUROC by 3.5 3.5 points, and direct pseudo-mask–proposal agreement reaches 0.806 0.806 , so ρ i \rho_{i} adds 2.1 2.1 points over direct external checking and the gain comes from fusing external and internal evidence, not from either alone. On naturally occurring pseudo-labels (Table XXV (a)), quality decreases monotonically across the five ρ i \rho_{i} quintiles, with a 32.2 32.2 -point top-to-bottom IoU gap and a sample-level Spearman correlation of 0.64 0.64 with true IoU. Thus, in the pseudo-label regime, ρ i \rho_{i} ranks true supervision quality beyond model confidence.

sections.heading: IV-K 2 Does the temporal weight align with useful updates
sections.text: On a fixed diagnostic subset 𝒟 s \mathcal{D}_{s} , we compare sample scores against an optimizer-conditioned first-order alignment proxy A i opt A_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}} , measured against a 200 200 -image probe set 𝒟 p \mathcal{D}_{p} held out from optimization and tuning. The proxy uses the unweighted loss and a frozen Adam preconditioner, so no compared weighting enters its own target. Correlations are computed independently over the four Phase-I refresh checkpoints with at least two history entries and then averaged. Full protocol details are in the Supp. Table XXV (b) shows that instantaneous loss is negatively correlated with update alignment, whereas ρ i \rho_{i} is moderately positive and ω i \omega_{i} achieves the strongest correlation and top- 20 % 20\% overlap. The two therefore answer different questions: ρ i \rho_{i} asks whether supervision can be trusted, and ω i \omega_{i} asks whether a sample is worth updating on now.

sections.heading: IV-K 3 Does the guard select the better mask, and does the challenge reduce high-frequency reliance
sections.text: Guard selection. We evaluate samples for which Q sup Q_{\mathrm{sup}} is surrogate-based, namely semi-supervised unlabeled and point-supervised samples. Selection is scored by post-hoc Top-1 accuracy, the fraction for which m + m^{+} is within 10 − 3 10^{-3} of the highest true IoU among the three candidates, and by regret max r ⁡ IoU ⁡ ( m r , y ) − IoU ⁡ ( m + , y ) \max_{r}\mathrm{IoU}(m^{r},y)-\mathrm{IoU}(m^{+},y) . Table XXVI shows that the full guard halves regret or better relative to the better single-cue rule, substantially exceeds the uniform-random Top-1 baseline, and improves over the guard without Q sup Q_{\mathrm{sup}} . Confidence is the weaker single cue, and consistency performs better but can still favor stable errors. Selection is also not trivial: the clean candidate accounts for at most 42 % 42\% of selections. Frequency intervention. We probe frequency reliance at an unseen cutoff of 0.70 0.70 of the Nyquist radius, outside the training radii { 0.90 , 0.95 , 1.00 } \{0.90,0.95,1.00\} , using high-frequency removal, low-frequency suppression, and band-limited high-frequency noise, with full protocol details in the Supp. Table XXVII reports drops relative to each model’s clean score. Relative to standard training, PaceShift reduces sensitivity to high-frequency removal and noise by 43 % 43\% and 45 % 45\% , while becoming more sensitive to low-frequency suppression, consistent with reduced reliance on high-frequency content. Naive easy-first training is both less accurate and more sensitive to the high-frequency interventions, consistent with the shortcut hypothesis.

sections.heading: V-A Why the Paradigm Works
sections.text: The diagnostics of Sec. IV-K say more when considered together than separately. Reliability and update value are two different quantities: ρ i \rho_{i} ranks held-out target quality more effectively than the evaluated confidence-based criteria (Tables XXV (a) and XIII ), whereas ω i \omega_{i} is the score most positively associated with the optimizer-conditioned alignment proxy, and instantaneous loss is negatively associated with it (Table XXV (b)). The guard selects low-regret candidates that confidence alone would not (Table XXVI ), both phases reduce high-frequency sensitivity (Table XXVII ), and the proposed order outperforms reversed and challenge-first schedules (Table XXII ). Together, these diagnostics support treating training order, supervision reliability, and post-training calibration as connected aspects of the training design.

sections.heading: V-B Scope and Limitations
sections.text: Spectral intervention is most useful when targets and backgrounds share low-level statistics, as in camouflaged, polyp, and transparent segmentation, and this mechanism is most directly supported by the CECS diagnostics. The broader experiments evaluate the full training recipe without isolating the contribution of each phase (Table IX ). When an object occupies only a few pixels, spectral attenuation may remove useful target evidence along with nuisance cues, and residual failures also include overlapping instances and heavy occlusion (see the Supp.). Reliability-aware scheduling may offer smaller gains when sample reliability varies little, and incomplete-supervision settings that use external teacher or proposal evidence depend on its quality. Finally, Phase II adds modest training-time computation (Table III ) but no inference-time parameters or cost.

sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: PaceShift turns CurriSeg’s setting-specific training recipe into a unified supervision-adaptive formulation and replaces its unguarded single-radius post-training with guarded multi-radius preference learning. Across CECS tasks, incomplete supervision, foundation-model adaptation, and broader dense prediction, it improves accuracy, and targeted evaluations show improved pooled calibration and corruption robustness in the evaluated settings and support the proposed mechanism.

Abstract Curriculum learning orders samples by difficulty, but difficulty alone does not establish supervision reliability for dense prediction. Easy samples can expose shortcuts, hard samples can be informative, and noisy or ambiguous samples can mislead training. Building on our conference method CurriSeg, we present PaceShift, a stabilize-then-challenge paradigm combining supervision-adaptive curriculum selection with guarded spectral post-training. A learning-dynamics view motivates separating supervision reliability from temporal update value and applying spectral challenges after stabilization. The first phase estimates reliability from available supervision, augmentation consistency, model disagreement, and prediction certainty. Temporal statistics guide sample weighting, while pixel-uncertainty weights reduce the early influence of uncertain regions. The second phase ranks predictions from multiple spectral views using supervision agreement, robustness, reference consistency, and penalties. A pairwise preference objective measured against the frozen Phase-I reference, together with an anchor, refines the prediction. The framework supports full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision. Experiments across context-entangled content segmentation (CECS), broader dense-prediction tasks, and foundation-model and cross-modal adaptations show accuracy gains. Targeted diagnostics indicate improved pooled calibration and corruption robustness in the evaluated settings. PaceShift preserves the deployed architecture and adds no inference computation. Code will be publicly released. I Introduction Dense prediction assigns a structured label to every pixel and underpins perception across medical, autonomous, and industrial applications [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Most progress has been architectural: stronger backbones [ 6 ] , dedicated detectors with multi-scale aggregation [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , attention [ 10 ] , and frequency-aware modules [ 11 ] . We instead argue that dense prediction is limited not only by network capacity but also by training-signal reliability and the order in which it is consumed (Fig. ). Fig. 2: Curriculum paradigms for dense prediction. A naive curriculum orders samples easy-to-hard by a static ground-truth difficulty and can strengthen reliance on fragile texture cues. CurriSeg adds temporal statistics and a stabilize-then-challenge schedule, but its score is defined by dense-mask error and its single-radius challenge is unguarded. PaceShift keeps the same overall two-phase training skeleton and changes two core components: a four-cue supervision-adaptive score ρ i \rho_{i} and a guarded multi-radius spectral challenge during post-training, without changing the deployed model architecture. The reliability problem is sharpest in context-entangled content segmentation (CECS), where objects share intrinsic visual patterns with their background, as in camouflaged object detection [ 7 ] , transparent object detection [ 12 ] , and concealed defect detection [ 4 , 13 ] . We also include polyp segmentation as a CECS-related task with low boundary contrast, local ambiguity, and annotation uncertainty. Existing methods address the resulting feature ambiguity mainly by enhancing representations [ 11 , 14 ] . Yet a more basic bottleneck is the learning dynamics that arise when the data distribution is entangled. We make this concrete with three observations that, while most visible in CECS, recur across dense prediction. Difficulty and learning value are not the same quantity. Curriculum learning [ 15 ] typically orders samples from easy to hard, but in CECS, apparent easiness can arise from residual texture contrast that reveals the object. Prioritizing samples with low loss or error may therefore encourage reliance on fragile high-frequency cues instead of shape and context. This concern is supported by our experiments: under a matched budget, naive easy-to-hard ordering performs no better than random ordering, while conventional schedules can reduce accuracy. Frequency-intervention results further show greater sensitivity to high-frequency perturbations after naive easy-first training. Hard samples pose a complementary challenge: high prediction error can reflect either informative visual difficulty or unreliable supervision. A well-concealed object may be difficult yet informative, whereas weak annotations, imperfect ground-truth quality [ 16 ] , label drift, or intrinsically ambiguous regions can produce high errors without equally useful training signals. Since a static difficulty score cannot reliably distinguish these cases, difficulty-based selection may discard informative samples while retaining unreliable ones, increasing the risk of overfitting. Confidence, finally, is not reliability. Uncertain boundary and low-contrast regions can dominate early gradients, while high confidence need not imply correctness. Directly rewarding confidence can therefore reinforce errors and degrade calibration. Together, these three observations suggest that reliable training must distinguish supervision quality from temporal learning value, regulate uncertain pixels, and challenge shortcut reliance only after initial stabilization is reached. From CurriSeg to PaceShift. Our conference work CurriSeg [ 17 ] , published at ICML 2026, introduced a two-phase stabilize-then-challenge framework for CECS. It combined dense-mask difficulty trajectories, temporal sample weighting, pixel uncertainty weighting, and single-radius spectral-blindness fine-tuning (SBFT). However, its difficulty score required dense ground-truth masks and could not be applied uniformly across weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision. Moreover, its single-radius spectral stage lacked a mechanism for assessing the reliability of alternative predictions. To address these limitations, we develop PaceShift (Fig. 2 ), which retains the two-phase design while introducing supervision-adaptive curriculum selection and guarded multi-radius post-training with reference-relative preference learning. These changes extend the training framework without modifying the deployed architecture or increasing inference cost. Scope. CECS serves as our primary setting for studying supervision reliability and texture shortcuts together. Experiments on broader dense-prediction tasks evaluate the transfer of the full training framework, while mechanism-specific evidence is established primarily in CECS and unreliable-supervision settings. This paper makes four contributions: (1) A learning-dynamics view of dense prediction (Sec. III-B ). We explain why naive easy-first curricula can amplify fragile shortcuts and why the stabilize-then-challenge framework succeeds, separating supervision reliability from temporal update value and treating SBFT as a post-stabilization frequency bottleneck whose order matters. (2) Supervision-adaptive curriculum selection (Sec. III-C ). We replace ground-truth difficulty with a reliability score combining available supervision, augmentation consistency, model disagreement, and prediction uncertainty, yielding one curriculum under full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision while reducing confirmation bias. (3) Guarded anti-curriculum post-training (Sec. III-D ). SBFT-P (SBFT with preference-guarded post-training) combines multi-radius spectral challenges with a supervision-adaptive preference guard based on correctness, robustness, and consistency, with uncertainty as a weak penalty and not as the sole selection rule, improving robustness while reducing overconfidence in the evaluated settings and recovering the original SBFT as a special case under full supervision. (4) Systematic validation and diagnostics (Sec. IV ). We evaluate PaceShift across multiple dense-prediction families, supervision regimes, architectures, data-centric baselines, and foundation-model and cross-modal settings. Targeted experiments examine training dynamics, supervision reliability, candidate selection, corruption robustness, and calibration without additional inference computation. Beyond the methodological changes, this journal extension substantially expands the evaluation of CurriSeg [ 17 ] . We extend the broader dense-prediction evaluation to clinical, dichotomous, and salient segmentation; add vision-language and reference-guided evaluations; expand data-centric comparisons; and report paired-run statistical tests. Targeted analyses of supervision reliability, temporal update value, guard selection, phase ordering, frequency sensitivity, corruption robustness, and calibration further examine the underlying mechanisms. II Related Work Context-entangled and dense prediction segmentation. CECS spans camouflaged object detection [ 3 , 18 ] , transparent object detection [ 19 ] , and concealed defect detection [ 13 ] , with polyp segmentation [ 20 ] as a closely related low-contrast task. Progress has been mostly architectural: encoder-decoder backbones with multi-scale aggregation [ 7 ] , attention-based refinement [ 9 ] , edge- or uncertainty-aware branches [ 10 , 21 ] , transformer context modeling [ 22 ] , and frequency-aware modules [ 11 ] . These works strengthen representation but keep a standard supervised routine with shuffled mini-batches, so the roles of sample difficulty, label ambiguity, and texture shortcuts in the learning dynamics remain underexplored. Reversible unfolding [ 12 ] and nested unfolding [ 14 ] designs have begun to inject inductive structure into the decoder, yet the optimization schedule itself is rarely treated as an explicit design variable. Curriculum learning and self-paced learning. Curriculum learning orders training from easy to hard to improve generalization [ 15 , 23 ] , with variants in self-paced learning [ 24 ] , teacher-student curricula [ 25 , 26 ] , and loss- or hardness-based ranking [ 27 , 28 ] . These methods assume that easy samples give reliable supervision and that difficulty tracks learning utility. Both break in CECS: easy samples may carry spurious texture that promotes shortcuts, and hard samples can be at once informative and ambiguous, consistent with analyses showing that the benefit of ordering depends sharply on data structure [ 26 ] . Most curricula also ignore the pixel-level uncertainty of dense prediction, and almost none deliberately increase difficulty after a stable solution is reached. PaceShift instead separates reliability from temporal update value, extends the curriculum to pixels, and introduces a post-stabilization anti-curriculum. Data-centric learning: training dynamics and data efficiency. Training-dynamics methods characterize examples through evolving predictions, losses, margins, or gradients, including forgetting events [ 29 , 30 ] , EL2N and GraNd [ 31 ] , dataset cartography [ 32 ] , and AUM [ 33 ] . Dyn-Unc [ 34 ] and TDDS [ 35 ] further exploit temporal variability, while InfoBatch [ 36 ] and SeTa [ 37 ] dynamically remove low-value samples for efficiency. ADELE [ 38 ] instead uses early-learning dynamics to correct noisy labels. Most of these formulations assume sample-level labels and do not directly address sparse, pixel-level, or model-derived supervision. PaceShift builds on this line of work but derives the trajectory from supervision-adaptive dense reliability, couples it with pixel-level uncertainty, and follows stabilization with guarded post-training. Its aim is accuracy, robustness, and calibration under spatially and supervision-dependent unreliability, not pruning or label correction. Learning under incomplete supervision. Weakly and semi-supervised segmentation learn from sparse annotations or unlabeled data through consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling [ 39 , 40 ] . A recurring failure is confirmation bias: training on the model’s own confident predictions reinforces existing errors [ 41 ] . In CECS this is acute, since confidence and correctness diverge in concealed regions, so a confidence threshold both keeps wrong pseudo-labels and discards hard but correct ones. PaceShift instead combines confidence, disagreement, consistency, and an external foundation-model cue for reliability estimation, whereas SEE [ 42 ] generates changing pseudo-labels from a frozen SAM and SCALER [ 43 ] jointly adapts SAM and the segmenter. Shortcut bias, texture bias, and frequency-domain learning. Networks trained by SGD favor the simplest features that separate the data even when more robust ones exist, studied as simplicity bias [ 44 , 45 ] and, for vision, texture bias [ 46 ] . This differs from the spectral bias of network functions, which learn the low-frequency components of the input-output map first [ 47 ] . The two concern different frequencies, image versus function, and conflating them yields contradictory predictions about a low-pass operation. We therefore frame SBFT as suppressing a high-frequency image shortcut to counteract texture bias without invoking function-space spectral bias. Foundation-model adaptation and post-training. Segment-Anything-style models [ 48 ] are adapted to specialized domains through adapters, prompt modules, or low-rank updates [ 49 , 50 ] . Related segmentation systems condition on text or image prompts [ 51 , 52 ] , open-vocabulary alignment [ 53 ] , or reference images [ 54 ] . Such conditioning introduces another source of unreliability, namely the alignment between the conditioning signal and the predicted mask, which PaceShift treats as an additional reliability cue without adding a new mechanism. Separately, DPO [ 55 ] learns from preferred and dispreferred outputs without fitting a separate explicit reward model. We adopt a related pairwise objective for dense predictions and define preferences through correctness, robustness, and consistency on dense masks. Fig. 3: Framework of PaceShift. III-B A Learning-Dynamics View We first lay out the learning dynamics motivating the design. III-B 1 Easy samples amplify a high-frequency shortcut In a context-entangled scene, an object is concealed when its appearance matches the background. In CECS, one recurring source of apparent easiness is residual local high-frequency texture contrast that separates the object from its background. A model trained on these first can minimize the loss by keying on that texture difference, a feature that is cheap to fit and locally discriminative but does not transfer to well-concealed cases. This is an instance of simplicity and texture bias [ 44 ] : gradient descent prefers the simplest separating feature even when a more robust shape or context feature exists. This is not the classical spectral bias of network functions [ 47 , 56 ] , which concerns the order in which frequencies of the input-output map are learned. Here the relevant frequency is in image space, and the pathology is that early easy-first training increases reliance on a high-frequency image cue. This motivates the two phases: keep shortcut-prone easy samples from dominating early training, then suppress the high-frequency channel once a sufficiently stable representation exists. III-B 2 Temporal dynamics reveal update value A single difficulty value cannot tell an informative hard sample from a noisy one, while the training trajectory can. For sample i i let d i ( k ) d_{i}^{(k)} denote its difficulty at checkpoint k k . Two patterns are used as heuristics. A high variance of { d i ( k ) } k \{d_{i}^{(k)}\}_{k} reflects strong temporal variation, which is common near decision boundaries or under intrinsic ambiguity. A high mean with low variance reflects persistent failure, which can arise from outliers or label errors that the model cannot resolve, and the empirical rule down-weights it. This reading aligns with example-difficulty and forgetting analyses [ 29 , 31 ] and with Dyn-Unc and TDDS [ 34 , 35 ] , which likewise exploit training dynamics instead of a single value. We import neither score directly: we model the mean, the variance, and the persistent-failure pattern of high mean and low variance as separate, individually ablatable terms on the supervision-adaptive difficulty of Sec. This is what motivates the parameter-free mid-variance preference and the outlier penalty ω out \omega^{\mathrm{out}} in Sec. SBFT attenuates x hi x^{\mathrm{hi}} while requiring consistent prediction through the supervised or guarded objective, a frequency-level bottleneck inspired by, but not formally an instance of, the information bottleneck [ 57 ] . The phase order is not interchangeable: if the bottleneck is imposed before a stable representation exists, the model is deprived of the cues it needs to bootstrap structure, and applying the challenge directly after warm-up falls below standard training on every reported metric (Table XXII ).
